The backroom deal that built NYC’s omnipresent surveillance : Planet Money : NPR

Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
The backroom deal that built NYC’s omnipresent surveillance : Planet Money For years, police have spent billions of tax dollars on watching us, tracking us, and recording us. In the largest police department in the country, these surveillance systems were paid for and adopted without the kind of public oversight cities usually require.
In the wake of 9/11, the New York Police Department built one of the most sophisticated and omnipresent surveillance systems in the country.
And while decisions were being made about what tech to adopt and how much to pay for it, few outside the NYPD were consulted. Not the City Council nor the public. For over a decade, the only paper trail of these purchases were offline, stored in filing cabinets, inaccessible to the public.
Today on the show, how the country’s largest police department built its surveillance system, and the fight to get police everywhere to tell us how they’re watching us.

You're reading a newsletter from  The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter.  Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
Outside of Atlanta, two gas stations got into a price war. The Atlanta TV station WSB-TV reported that, over the course of a day, prices dropped from $2.54 down to $1.44, $1.39 and eventually down to just 97 cents. When drivers took notice, the traffic jam began and police intervened. BUT while it was happening, one driver said she only spent $15 to fill up her truck. It usually costs $90. "Look at God, baby! Look at God!" she said.
In our team's Slack, co-host Wailin Wong responded to the low prices, "make it up on volume!?" Jeff Guo wrote, "how is this real." But like, actually. How is this real?

Why websites make it hard to leave
What To Know: Social media sites don't love it when users leave. If you've ever used Instagram, it's not the easiest place to post links. You need to include them in bios, or through a special button on stories. Well now, if you run a Facebook page, you can only post TWO hyperlinks for free per month. $49.99/month will get you a Meta One Advanced plan, allowing you to include eight hyperlinks in posts or reels. With the $499/month Max plan, you can post an unlimited amount. Ashley Gullen, who runs a game design company, posted on Mastodon, a decentralized social media platform, "Facebook achieving absurd new heights of enshittification" in response to the news. This isn't totally unique. Nieman Lab did a whole study finding that posting links hurts news publishers on X.
Meta has limited how many hyperlinks Facebook Pages can post through a subscription
Tony Avelar/AP Photo
hide caption
Tony Avelar/AP Photo
Why are companies doing this?: Attention is money for social media sites. They want to keep you inside their walls! David Evans, managing director at BRG, a consulting firm, wrote a simple explanation as to why platforms want you to stay on their site: "Attention platforms use content to get consumers to spend time on their platform and sell marketers the ability to expose these consumers to messages."
Even FAKE data centers could be driving up electricity costs - The Wall Street Journal
What To Know: Developers are desperate to get their data centers up and running. They need it to help power their precious AI and whatever other computing is needed. BUT, developers won't just say, "This is the only location we'll accept for this project." No, they'll put out requests to all sorts of locations for their centers. The problem is, utilities are still considering data centers that likely WON'T GET BUILT in their electricity forecasts. Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie estimates that only a mere 23% of data-center requests are considered "high confidence," according to The Wall Street Journal. The rest are speculative!
How this affects YOU: Electricity costs could rise even if the data centers don't get built. Hoowwwwww does that work now? Because utilities are still planning for expected demand. They can't just suddenly integrate a wildly power-demanding data center without new substations or transmission lines. It's possible for the utility to pass on some of those grid investments onto consumers, even if the data centers never come to pass. Some power markets also set prices based on future demand so… There are lots of ways these projects could mess with your electricity bill.
Another oil reserve gets tapped - U.S. Department of Energy
It's your weekly update on diesel prices! This week, the Trump administration has found a NEW way to try and lower prices, which seems to be a core issue ahead of the midterms. This time, the U.S. Department of Energy has authorized an exchange from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve. It would release roughly a third of the reserves for heating oil. The Chief Energy Advisor for Gulf Oil thinks it won't make a difference on prices.
Tom Kloza is the chief energy advisor for Gulf Oil
Screenshot of a post on X by @tomkloza/X
hide caption
Screenshot of a post on X by @tomkloza/X
What's interesting, this reserve has only been tapped ONCE, and that was after Hurricane Sandy. According to the DOE's history, that's the sort of thing it was meant for. "The intent was to create a buffer large enough to allow commercial companies to compensate for interruptions in supply during severe winter weather." Here, the DOE will loan out up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil in hopes of lowering prices. It's called an exchange because borrowing entities, like a regional heating oil retailer, would be required to replace the same volume at a premium ahead of next year.

articles.title: Gen Z is 'in the thick' of high housing costs. These candidates aim to solve it
articles.text:
Gen Z candidates on housing and affordability : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Gen Z candidates on housing and affordability Young candidates who rent or live with parents say their generation is "in the thick" of the country's housing affordability crisis. They argue this gives them new energy to solve it for everyone.
Gen Z is 'in the thick' of high housing costs. These candidates aim to solve it
October 23, 20265:00 AM ET
Jennifer Ludden
Left: Democrat Olaleye Onikuyide, 28, is running for state representative in Connecticut. Right: Republican Lukas Schubert, 21, is campaigning for reelection as a state representative in Montana. Both candidates are focusing on a lack of affordable housing in their states.
Raquel C. Zaldívar and Sarah Mosquera for NPR
hide caption
Raquel C. Zaldívar and Sarah Mosquera for NPR
WEST HARTFORD, Conn. — "My bus is running slightly behind," Olaleye Onikuyide texted ahead of our meeting at a coffee shop on West Hartford's main street. The 28-year-old Democrat running for Connecticut state representative still made it on time and said he loved riding public transit.
Family
Amid cost-of-living stress, many parents are supporting children well into adulthood
Onikuyide also lives with his parents, though he said that's by choice to save money, unlike the many young adults who can't afford to live on their own.
Still, as part of a generation that faces record-high housing unaffordability, he started obsessing years ago over how to make it cheaper. Now that the cripplingly high cost of both rent and homes has become an urgent national conversation, he likens it to being a fan of a niche music group before everyone else caught on.
"All of a sudden, it's blown up and everybody's at the concerts and you're like, 'OK, this is a bit of a crowd here now,'" he said with a broad smile.
Onikuyide and his campaign manager, Karo Shakhnazarov, canvass in West Hartford, Connecticut.
Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
hide caption
Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
Nationwide, housing costs are a top issue for voters in a midterms season laser focused on affordability. A chronic housing shortage has pushed up prices, and the fallout cuts across generations.
Only on NPR
'Everything got worse': Gen Z expresses frustration, regret after Trump vote
Younger people are renting with roommates into their 30s. They're struggling to save for a down payment and wondering whether it even makes sense to buy, given today's sky-high prices. Empty nesters looking to downsize can't find an affordable place to go, and longtime homeowners are reluctant to move at all, given current high mortgage rates.
Generation Z candidates from both major parties said their age group has a lot at stake and is uniquely positioned to help create solutions for everyone.
"We're in the thick of it," Onikuyide said, citing not only high housing and gas prices but also student loan debt and a tough labor market. "We might be the generation that is more educated and yet worse off than our parents."
Onikuyide leaves information about his campaign at a voter's home in West Hartford. He appreciates the national debate on high housing costs but says the action to address it is happening at the state level.
Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
hide caption
Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
His policy goals include creating more mixed-income housing and walkable cities. Adding density to urban areas can be controversial, as longtime residents worry about more traffic or strained infrastructure. But Onikuyide and others also see an opportunity for bipartisanship. And if elected, he would feel well-placed to make life less expensive for his constituents.
"I keep one eye on the national conversation about it," he said, "but the action is happening at the state level."
"The experience of being a renter"
About an hour away in New Haven, Conn., 26-year-old Eli Sabin found a quiet room for talking inside the ornate City Hall. He's also a Democrat running for state representative, and he has worked in this building.
When he was a sophomore in college, he started serving on the Board of Alders. That's "our old-fashioned term for the city council," he explained. "We changed some of the zoning rules to allow for denser development and more affordable units."
Democrat Eli Sabin, 26, is running for state representative in Connecticut. He feels his experience as a renter is important, since elected officials at all levels in the U.S. are overwhelmingly homeowners.
Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
hide caption
Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
Elected officials at all levels in the U.S. are overwhelmingly homeowners. Sabin said it makes a difference that he is a renter, like about 70% of residents in this city.
"I think it's the experience of being a renter and just the insecurity and instability that you feel," he said. His lease is up in May, and he has no idea whether the rent will go up or whether the landlord will even allow him to stay.
Economy
It's getting harder to afford rent in the U.S., even for middle-income families
Economy
The renter-owner wealth gap is wider than ever, as many are priced out of buying
He would like more protections against eviction and would also like to make it easier to buy a home.
Older people have told him how they bought 30 years ago on a teacher's salary but could never do that today, while younger people feel "pushed out of the community." Some have moved to states such as Texas, Tennessee or Florida, "not because that's where they have the best job opportunities or where they want to be, but because simply that's the place they can afford," he said.
New Haven resident James Fripp Jr. (left) speaks with Sabin.
Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR
hide caption
Raquel C. Zaldívar for NPR

articles.title: How America's mahjong craze is throwing a Chinese manufacturing town a lifeline
articles.text:
U.S. mahjong craze throws China manufacturing town lifeline : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
U.S. mahjong craze throws China manufacturing town lifeline Shoppers in the U.S. are willing to spend hundreds of dollars for a mahjong set. In the eastern Chinese city of Taixing, manufacturers can barely keep up with the demand.
How America's mahjong craze is throwing a Chinese manufacturing town a lifeline
Updated October 24, 20266:00 AM ET
Originally published October 22, 20264:53 PM ET
Heard on All Things Considered
Jennifer Pak
Chinese Mahjong town
Listen
4:58
4:58
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6000127/nx-s1-9974942" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
A worker in a mahjong workshop in Taixing, China, inspects each tile to ensure there are no imperfections before they're shipped off to the U.S. and sold for hundreds of dollars a set.
Jasmine Ling/NPR
hide caption
Jasmine Ling/NPR
TAIXING, China — In the eastern Chinese city of Taixing, a two-story village home doubles as a workshop manufacturing mahjong — a Chinese tile-based game that's having a moment in the United States.
Inside, three workers at Taixing Senju Cultural Entertainment Supplies arrange burnt-orange and pearl-white tiles on wooden boards, holding them against the light. They press their noses close to the tiles, inspecting every edge. When they spot an imperfection, the tile drops into a milk crate.
Every piece must be perfect because these tiles are headed to the U.S.
"Our clients are selling these mahjong sets for $300 to $400, sometimes more. We make it for them for about 200 yuan [$30] a set," said workshop co-owner Wang Hao.
Games
How people are finding community through the tile game Mahjong
At such high profit margins, Wang said their clients, who are mainly Amazon vendors, are not complaining about U.S. tariffs or surging shipping costs brought by conflicts in the Middle East and Europe.
Mahjong started in China in the late 1800s and spread to the U.S. in the 1920s. It has seen a revival recently thanks to social media. While working at e-commerce giant Alibaba.com, Wang noticed the search volume for mahjong surged over 1,000% late last year. He quit his job to start distributing mahjong to the U.S., where they play a different style than the one in China.
The mahjong sets trending in the U.S. are smaller and more colorful than traditional mahjong sold in China. American-style mahjong tiles are made from acrylic — a material that requires different production techniques and machinery.
Jasmine Ling/NPR
hide caption
Jasmine Ling/NPR
While geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions have squeezed profits across much of China's exporting sector, an unexpected craze for mahjong in the U.S. has delivered a boost to Taixing's tile makers.
Local producers say they can hardly keep up with the orders.
It is partly why Wang expanded beyond distribution into direct manufacturing. "When I started selling last year, the supply of mahjong was tight. Even if I paid the factory [way in advance], it wouldn't necessarily guarantee I'd get the shipment on time," he said.
Overhauling the craftsmanship
Wang Hao holds up a set of his workshop's mahjong designs designated for the U.S. market. He expanded beyond distribution into direct manufacturing because producers in Taixing could not keep up with U.S. demand.
Jasmine Ling/NPR
hide caption
Jasmine Ling/NPR
Meeting American demand, however, requires a complete overhaul of the craftsmanship. Traditional mahjong sets are usually made from melamine, which gives the tiles a heavy, stone-like feel and produces a smooth clack when shuffled.
American buyers, Wang noted, prefer smaller, more colorful tiles made from acrylic, a material that requires different production techniques and machinery.
One early adopter was Zhu Xingyao, a second-generation maker who runs Taixing City Jiale Melamine Products. From the 1970s until recently, Zhu's family business primarily served the domestic Chinese market.
Code Switch
Keep culture and tradition alive at the mahjong table
Today, almost every set rolling off his line is bound for overseas: sparkly red and seafoam green acrylic tiles engraved with flowers and Christmas motifs like Santa Claus.
The booming overseas demand has made Zhu largely abandon the domestic market. Chinese mahjong sales peaked between 2020 and 2022, when millions were locked down at home during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to Zhu.
Since then, Chinese consumers have been less willing to spend. In September, retail sales — a proxy for consumption — were barely up at 1.1%, the government reported.
"Involution," mahjong style
Second-generation mahjong manufacturer Zhu Xingyao, shown at his factory, was among the first to adapt his production line to produce American-style mahjong sets last year.
Jasmine Ling/NPR
hide caption
Jasmine Ling/NPR
Yet, even as domestic demand cooled, the number of mahjong manufacturers grew. "The cake is only so big, and everyone wants a slice, so the [Chinese] market became cutthroat," Zhu said.
In China, the phenomenon is called neijuan, or "involution," a buzzword describing intense competition. It has hit nearly every sector of the Chinese economy, and in Taixing, Zhu said, the competition comes from former co-workers.
Word of the week
Feeling burned out? There's a word for that in Mandarin Chinese
"People who used to work in our factory saw we could barely keep up with demand. So, they'd go back to their hometowns and set up their own factories with relatives in places such as Henan and Anhui," Zhu told NPR. "Wages are lower there."
The cheaper labor costs allow upstart competitors to undercut Zhu by a dollar or two per set. And scaled across orders of tens of thousands of units, that price gap matters to domestic buyers.

articles.title: Achy from sitting at a desk all day? Try doing this
articles.text:
Sitting at a desk all day hurts. 5 solutions to relieve aches and pains : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Sitting at a desk all day hurts. 5 solutions to relieve aches and pains Sitting at a desk all day hurts. And it isn't good for us. Strategies to make it a little more comfortable, from eye muscle exercises to alleviate eye strain to a back pain-fighting body movement.
Achy from sitting at a desk all day? Try doing this
October 22, 20265:01 AM ET
By
Malaka Gharib
Marielle Segarra
Andee Tagle
Life Kit
Olga Pankova/Getty Images/Moment RF
Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.
If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.
But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.
Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.
If you feel tired and sluggish … go for a five-minute walk (every half hour)
Antonio_Diaz/Getty Images/iStockphoto
We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.
But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy.
In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue.
Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks.
If your back aches from slouching over your desk … rotate your spine
Beck Harlan/NPR
Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.
This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.
To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.
For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.
If your eyes hurt from staring at a screen … stretch your eye muscles
When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.
Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.
LA Johnson/NPR
If you feel fidgety and restless … change your position (and don't worry too much about the "right" posture)
ljubaphoto/Getty Images/E+
Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman, a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters. Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough.
So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.
The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek, a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.
Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."
If sitting at your desk makes you feel uncomfortable … adjust your workspace
LA Johnson/NPR
Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.
Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.
Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just he
